title: Singing it for someone
hook: a shabad sung for a sick or grieving friend is a gift

segments.voice: Yesterday, kanth, and your line: by heart. Did your two lines stay with you? It's the end of a week that made the forest at home, sang laments, honored the brave, kept a shabad for the house, chose the right song and learned it by heart. Today: give it away. Day six hundred seventy-nine.
screen: `THE FOREST AT HOME · ALL MUST GO · ACCEPTED · OUR SHABAD · THE RIGHT SONG · BY HEART.`

segments.voice: What do you say to a friend whose father just died? What do you bring to a hospital room? Flowers wilt, food piles up, and words come out wrong. Even a kind text can feel thin. Some Sikh families have an old answer. They sit by the bed, or in the living room of the grieving house, and they sing. Not performers. Aunties, cousins, a neighbor with a harmonium. Today: singing it for someone.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU SAY?` → `FLOWERS WILT, WORDS COME OUT WRONG.` → `SO THEY SING.`

segments.voice: In Sikh life, a shabad can be a gift you give with your voice. When someone is ill, families often gather for a reading of Sukhmani Sahib, the Psalm of Peace, or for kirtan at home, and end with an Ardas asking for the person's wellbeing. When someone has died, the sangat gathers at the family's house in the days that follow, for readings and kirtan, so the family isn't alone with the silence. What gets sung? Often a shabad of comfort. One line often turned to in illness comes from Sukhmani Sahib, on Ang two seventy-four. In paraphrase: the Name is the medicine for every illness. Others sing the hot wind that doesn't touch, or the Name that destroys pain. Why singing, and not just talking? A few reasons Sikhs give. First, the words aren't yours. You don't have to find the perfect thing to say; the Guru has already said it. Second, singing is shared. The sick person can listen with their eyes closed, and nobody has to make conversation. Third, it carries something beyond the singer. Sikhs understand the shabad as the Guru's own voice, so singing it for someone is offering them the Guru's company, not just your own. And here's the quiet part: it doesn't have to be good. A wobbly voice, a phone playing a recording, a line whispered at a bedside. The gift is the attention, and the Word.
screen: `A GIFT GIVEN WITH YOUR VOICE.` · `SUKHMANI AND KIRTAN AT HOME.` · `THE NAME, MEDICINE FOR ILLNESS.` · `IT DOESN'T HAVE TO BE GOOD.` · then, large: `SING IT FOR THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing or send one. Sit and think of someone who's sick, tired or grieving right now. Picture their face. Then take your two lines from yesterday, or any line you love, and say or hum them softly, as if for that person. Don't worry how it sounds. After the bell, if it feels right, send them the line, a recording, or just a note saying you thought of them. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them. The bell holds the time.
Aukhad, medicine: a shabad given to a sick or grieving friend is medicine too, the Guru's words offered with your own voice, however it sounds.
Your line: sing it for them. Today, send one line of comfort to someone who's having a hard time, in words that aren't yours. Day six hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: When someone is ill or has died, Sikh families and friends often gather at home for Sukhmani Sahib, kirtan and Ardas, singing shabads of comfort for the person and the family.
